newsitem.title: USA: Albright hopes for NATO-Russia charter.
newsitem.headline: Albright hopes for NATO-Russia charter.

text.p: Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said on Thursday she hoped a NATO-Russia security charter would be ready for signing next month but NATO expansion will proceed with or without the charter.
Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov said in Paris on Wednesday that President Boris Yeltsin had accepted a French invitation to a charter-signing ceremony in Paris on May 27.
That announcement took U.S. officials by surprise.

The prospective charter would codify terms of association between Russia and an expanded NATO that will soon include some of Moscow's former East European allies. It was conceived as a way of easing fierce Russian opposition to the expansion.

"We'd like to have that be so but whether it (the charter) is ready or not, we will go forward with NATO enlargement (at a NATO summit) in Madrid in July," Albright told a meeting of the American Society of Newspaper Editors.
She and other officials said negotiations between the alliance and Moscow on the charter are still underway, suggesting a positive outcome is not yet certain.
The United States is the biggest proponent of adding new East European members to the alliance and has long insisted that must proceed with or without a Russia-NATO accord.
Albright's decision to underscore that point seemed to indicate the two sides are not as close to an agreement as the Primakov's upbeat comments might suggest.

That impression was reinforced by State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns, who told reporters: "We do hope very much we'll be able to conclude this charter negotiation, but there is additional work to do ... NATO has not yet fully agreed with Russia."
Burns added: "Let's hope that some of the optimism in Paris yesterday turns out to be concrete results."
He also said that despite Primakov's announcement, it had not yet been decided where a signing ceremony would be held. "We're open to a lot of different possibilities," Burns said.
Albright spoke several hours after a meeting with NATO Secretary General Javier Solana, who is leading the alliance negotiations with Russia on the charter.

Solana declined to talk with reporters after two hours at the State Department, including talks with other top U.S. experts on Russia and arms control policies. He was expected to be in Moscow for more talks with that side next week.
Burns said Albright and Solana "discussed the course of the charter negotiations with Russia."
NATO leaders are due to meet in Madrid in July to decide which former Warsaw Pact countries will be formally invited to join the alliance as its first post-Cold War members.
Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are considered certain but Romania and Slovenia are also under consideration.

At a summit with Clinton in Helsinki last month, Yeltsin maintained Russia's strong opposition to the expansion. But he agreed to work with the alliance on a document -- the charter -- designed to ensure NATO-Russia cooperation as a foundation of European security into the next century.
The hope is for Yeltsin and leaders of the existing 16 NATO states to sign it before the Madrid summit if possible.
Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Georgy Mamedov is in Washington this week for talks with senior U.S. officials on the charter and a number of other issues.
